newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam dong slips to new floor against dollar.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam dong slips to new floor against dollar.

text.p: The Vietnamese dong slipped to the bottom of its new, wider trading band on Thursday, prompting speculation about the central bank's next move to accommodate continued corporate demand for the U.S. dollar.
"We're getting headaches today bouncing off the ceiling," said Peter McLean, head of treasury at Standard Chartered Bank in Hanoi.
Almost two weeks ago the central State Bank of Vietnam widened the official fluctuation band for the dong to plus or minus 1.0 percent from plus or minus 0.5 percent.
The new band, like the previous one, has 11,030 per dollar as its pivot rate, with the upper end at 10,920 and the lower end at 11,140.

State-owned Vietcombank was quoting an interbank rate of 11,098/105 dong per dollar on Tuesday, still some way off the new dollar ceiling of 11,140. But foreign banks were quoting the dong at 11,125/36 and 11,130/40 per dollar.
"It's gone to the top, we are there already," said one treasury expert at a European bank in Ho Chi Minh City.
He said liquidity may now dry up, as it did before the central bank widened the trading band at the end of last month.
Traders said the bank may sell dollars to bring the dong off the bottom of its official range or raise the pivot rate.

However, they said it may be reluctant to raise the pivot rate because that could signal a devaluation, a move the authorities toyed with as a quick-fix for the country's widening trade gap but eventually rejected.
"If they were seen to be moving the central rate higher, they would be seen as going back on their promise not to devalue," said one trader.

He added that corporate demand for dollars was to be expected ahead of the year-end, but predicted that demand for the local currency would return ahead of the Lunar New Year festival, which falls in early February next year.

Nevertheless, analysts still expect the authorities to implement a policy of very gradual depreciation. Standard Chartered's McLean said he was forecasting a dong depreciation of about one percent a quarter in 1997.
